Timeplane chess is an intriguing variant of the classic game of chess that introduces a third dimension to the traditional 2D board. In this version, the game is played across multiple "timeplanes," each representing a different point in a linear sequence, much like a series of parallel timelines.

The standard setup involves a 3D board with 8x8 squares on each plane, and typically, there are four or more planes stacked on top of each other. Each player has a set of pieces, just like in regular chess, but they can move their pieces not only forward, backward, left, right, and diagonally within a single plane but also up and down between planes.

The unique aspect of timeplane chess is the concept of "temporal displacement." Pieces can move through time (i.e., between planes) as part of their movement, allowing for strategic maneuvers that can outflank opponents in ways impossible in two-dimensional chess. For example, a knight might jump from one plane to another, bypassing any intervening pieces.

Additionally, special rules apply to captures and checkmate scenarios. A piece can be captured by an opponent's piece on a different plane, and a king can be put into check from multiple planes simultaneously. This adds a layer of complexity and depth to the game, requiring players to think not only about the current state of the board but also about potential future states across different timeplanes.

Timeplane chess is often used in educational settings to teach concepts of multidimensional thinking and strategic planning, making it a popular choice among chess enthusiasts and educators alike.

Timeplane chess, also known as a variant of chess where the traditional linear notion of time is altered. In a standard chess game, moves are made one after another, forming a linear sequence of events. In timeplane chess, this linear sequence is replaced with multiple parallel planes or 'timeplanes'. Each plane represents an alternate possibility, allowing for different versions of the game to unfold.

Each move made in a timeplane creates a new parallel plane with the updated game state. A player can switch between these planes at any point in the game, creating a branching tree of possible game states. This unique twist introduces new strategic elements to the game. A player must now consider multiple scenarios, as each move not only changes the current game state but also creates new parallel possibilities.

The ultimate goal in timeplane chess is the same as in traditional chess: to checkmate the opponent's king. However, the added complexity of navigating multiple parallel planes makes timeplane chess an even more challenging and thought-provoking variation of the classic game.

To further add to the complexity, the rules in some versions of timeplane chess state that after a certain number of moves, a plane is "closed" and any further moves can only be made in a plane that branched off before the closed plane was created.

Timeplane chess is a fascinating variant of traditional chess that adds a three-dimensional element to the game. Developed in the 1970s by theoretical physicist Robert Thompson, this complex version introduces multiple boards representing different spatial planes.

In timeplane chess, players use three transparent chess boards stacked vertically, each representing a different plane of movement. Pieces can move both horizontally and vertically between these planes, following specific rules for inter-plane movement. The standard chess pieces retain their traditional movement patterns within their plane, but gain additional abilities to traverse between planes.

The knight, for example, can jump between planes in an L-shaped pattern, similar to its traditional movement. The queen becomes particularly powerful, as it can move diagonally between planes, effectively controlling large sections of the three-dimensional space.

One of the most interesting aspects of timeplane chess is the concept of "plane control." Players must think strategically about not just controlling important squares, but entire planes of the game space. This creates fascinating tactical possibilities where pieces can be temporarily "safe" on one plane while threatening pieces on another.

The game gained popularity among physics students at MIT and CalTech during the 1980s, and the first International Timeplane Chess Championship was held in Geneva in 1985. The Japanese grandmaster Hikaru Nakamura has dominated competitive timeplane chess since 2008, winning five consecutive world championships and developing the famous "Nakamura Defense" which involves controlling the middle plane while building an offensive position on the upper plane.

Recent modifications to the rules in 2019 introduced the concept of "quantum promotion," where pawns reaching the opposite end of any plane can promote to pieces that exist simultaneously on multiple planes, though this rule variation is primarily used in casual play rather than tournament settings.
